title: Is the animal speed infographic a bar graph?
description: An infographic of animal speeds is checked for its scale, searched for a pair where one speed is about twice the other, and tested on two claims about the sailfish.
teaching_notes: One idea: a graph is read with its scale, and it can only support claims about the animals it actually shows. Watch for students who call a sailfish the fastest in the world from five animals.

source: Animal speeds in air, on land and in water: is it a bar graph, what is the scale, a pair where one speed is about twice the other, the sailfish against the humpback whale, and the fastest aquatic animal
video_script.why: The child can read a graph with its scale and now uses it to test a how many times claim.
video_script.substitution: Read each animal's length with the scale, then divide one speed by the other.
video_script.anchor: Infographic of animal speeds, equal scale steps of about 16 km/h. Estimates: peregrine falcon 322, swift 170, sailfish 109, flying fish 56, humpback whale 26.
video_script.payoff_line: The sailfish is about four times as fast as the humpback whale.

final_answer.value: Yes, a bar graph with steps of about 16 km/h; falcon and swift are about twice; sailfish is about 4 times the humpback whale (109 / 26 = 4.19); fastest in the world cannot be told from five animals
final_answer.spoken: it is a bar graph; the sailfish is about four times the humpback whale; fastest in the world cannot be told

maths_rules: scale: equal steps of about 16 km/h
pair about twice: falcon 322 and swift 170, 2 x 170 = 340, close to 322
sailfish 109 (accept 105 to 113) and humpback whale 26 (accept 22 to 30): 109 / 26 = 4.19, about 4
five water animals cannot show the fastest in the world
video_script.design: One idea: read lengths with the scale and claim only what the data shows. The infographic sits in the anchor; on the board two speeds are set side by side and divided.
open_questions: The animal speeds (falcon 322, swift 170, sailfish 109, humpback 26) are estimates from the worklist; the extracted book text has no readings for this infographic. Check against the printed infographic.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, check the scale.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The marks rise in equal steps of about sixteen kilometres per hour.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The length of each line stands for a speed, so yes, it is a bar graph.

marks.m1: the falcon and swift speeds are written side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, look for a pair where one speed is about twice the other.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The falcon is about three hundred and twenty two, and the swift about one hundred and seventy.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twice one hundred and seventy is three hundred and forty, which is close to the falcon.

marks.m2: 109 ÷ 26 is written with a question mark

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, test the claim about the sailfish. It is about one hundred and nine, and the humpback whale about twenty six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>To ask how many times, divide the sailfish speed by the whale speed.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check with a multiplication.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Four times twenty six is one hundred and four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is close to one hundred and nine.
